Tropical Weather Outlook
NWS Central Pacific Hurricane Center Honolulu HI
Issued by NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL
800 PM HST Thu Aug 20 2026

For the central North Pacific...between 140W and 180W:

Active Systems:
The National Hurricane Center is issuing advisories on Hurricane
Lala, located near Laysan Island, and on Tropical Depression Two-C,
located about 800 miles east-southeast of Hilo, Hawaii.

Tropical cyclone formation is not expected during the next 7 days.

&&

under WMO header WTPA33 PHFO and under AWIPS header HFOTCPCP3.

item.description:
Issued at 800 PM HST Thu Aug 20 2026 
000

BULLETIN
Hurricane Lala Intermediate Advisory Number 35A
NWS Central Pacific Hurricane Center Honolulu HI   CP012026
Issued by NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL
800 PM HST Thu Aug 20 2026
 
...LALA TURNS TOWARD THE NORTH-NORTHEAST...
...HURRICANE CONDITIONS CONTINUE WITHIN PORTIONS OF THE
PAPAHANAUMOKUAKEA MARINE NATIONAL MONUMENT...
 
 
SUMMARY OF 800 PM HST...0600 UTC...INFORMATION
----------------------------------------------
LOCATION...26.1N 172.0W
ABOUT 110 MI...175 KM WNW OF MARO REEF
ABOUT 125 MI...200 KM E OF LISIANSKI ISLAND
MAXIMUM SUSTAINED WINDS...90 MPH...150 KM/H
PRESENT MOVEMENT...NNE OR 15 DEGREES AT 10 MPH...17 KM/H
MINIMUM CENTRAL PRESSURE...974 MB...28.77 INCHES
 
 
WATCHES AND WARNINGS
--------------------
CHANGES WITH THIS ADVISORY:
 
None.
 
SUMMARY OF WATCHES AND WARNINGS IN EFFECT:
 
A Hurricane Warning is in effect for...
* The Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument from Lisianski
Island to Maro Reef
 
A Tropical Storm Warning is in effect for...
* The Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument east of Maro Reef
to French Frigate Shoals
 
A Hurricane Warning means that hurricane conditions are expected
somewhere within the warning area. 
 
A Tropical Storm Warning means that tropical storm conditions are
expected somewhere within the warning area.
 
For storm information specific to your area, including possible
inland watches and warnings, please monitor products issued by your
local National Weather Service forecast office.
 
 
DISCUSSION AND OUTLOOK
----------------------
At 800 PM HST (0600 UTC), the center of Hurricane Lala was located
near latitude 26.1 North, longitude 172.0 West. Lala is moving
toward the north-northeast near 10 mph (17 km/h). A turn toward 
the north is forecast later today, followed by a northwestward 
motion by this weekend. On the forecast track, the center of Lala 
will continue to traverse the Papahanaumokuakea Marine National 
Monument for the next couple of days.
 
Maximum sustained winds are near 90 mph (150 km/h) with higher
gusts.  Some intensity fluctuations are possible during the next 
day or so, followed by a gradual weakening trend. However, Lala is 
expected to remain a hurricane into the weekend.
 
Hurricane-force winds extend outward up to 45 miles (75 km) from
the center and tropical-storm-force winds extend outward up to 150
miles (240 km).
 
The estimated minimum central pressure is 974 mb (28.77 inches).
 
 
HAZARDS AFFECTING LAND
----------------------
WIND: Hurricane conditions are expected to continue within the
Hurricane Warning area into Friday. Tropical storm conditions are
currently occurring within the Tropical Storm Warning area and will
persist into Friday.
 
SURF: Large surf associated with Lala will affect the
Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument for the next couple of
days. These large waves will likely inundate some of the low-lying
atolls, especially from French Frigate Shoals to Maro Reef.
 
 
NEXT ADVISORY
-------------
Next complete advisory at 1100 PM HST.
 
$$
Forecaster Berg
item.author: nhcwebmaster@noaa.gov (NHC Webmaster)

item.title: Hurricane Lala Forecast Discussion Number 35
item.description:
Issued at 500 PM HST Thu Aug 20 2026 
305 
WTPA42 PHFO 210235
TCDCP2
 
Hurricane Lala Discussion Number  35
NWS Central Pacific Hurricane Center Honolulu HI   CP012026
Issued by NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL
500 PM HST Thu Aug 20 2026
 
Lala's satellite presentation has changed little during the past
several hours, characterized by a persistent band of deep convection
over the western semicircle of the inner core. While intermittent
dry air entrainment has occurred, the cyclone has successfully
fended off these intrusions before they could significantly disrupt
the overall structure.  The current Subjective and objective
satellite intensity estimates show a large spread, ranging from 65
to 92 kt. Given the relatively steady state of the system and a
blend of these estimates, the initial intensity is held at 80 kt for
this advisory.
 
The hurricane has made the anticipated turn toward the north, with
an estimated initial motion of 355/8 kt. This general heading should
continue for the next day or so. Thereafter, a large mid-level ridge
over the central Pacific is forecast to build to the northeast of
the system, which should cause Lala to turn back toward the
northwest. The track model guidance is in fairly good agreement
throughout the forecast period, with the primary spread consisting
of only minor along-track differences in forward speed. The updated
NHC track forecast is very similar to the previous advisory and lies
near the various multi-model consensus aids, including the GDMI.
 
Lala will remain a strong hurricane as it moves through the
Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument, passing near or over
some of the atolls tonight into tomorrow and lingering within the
monument area for the next couple of days. Intensity guidance
indicates that some fluctuations in strength are possible during the
next day or so. The cyclone is currently situated in an environment
with enhanced upper-level divergence, which is helping to offset the
negative impacts of moderate vertical wind shear and dry air. Thus,
the official intensity forecast shows little change in strength in
the short term. By this weekend, a gradual weakening trend should
commence, in agreement with the latest HCCA consensus aid, as the
favorable divergence aloft wanes and the shear and dry air begin to
take a greater toll on the system. In about 3 days, Lala is forecast
to move over increasingly cooler sea surface temperatures. The
combination of cooler waters, persistent shear, and a dry mid-level
environment should induce a steadier rate of weakening. Although the
official forecast does not explicitly depict Lala becoming a
post-tropical cyclone at the end of the forecast period, some global
models suggest the system could struggle to maintain organized deep
convection by Day 5.

item.description:
Issued at 500 PM HST Thu Aug 20 2026 
000
WTPA33 PHFO 210234
TCPCP3
 
BULLETIN
Tropical Depression Two-C Advisory Number   3
NWS Central Pacific Hurricane Center Honolulu HI   CP022026
Issued by NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL
500 PM HST Thu Aug 20 2026
 
...TROPICAL DEPRESSION COULD BRING HEAVY RAINFALL TO PORTIONS
OF THE HAWAIIAN ISLANDS THIS WEEKEND AND EARLY NEXT WEEK...
 
 
SUMMARY OF 500 PM HST...0300 UTC...INFORMATION
----------------------------------------------
LOCATION...12.9N 145.0W
ABOUT 815 MI...1315 KM SE OF HILO HAWAII
MAXIMUM SUSTAINED WINDS...35 MPH...55 KM/H
PRESENT MOVEMENT...WNW OR 290 DEGREES AT 14 MPH...22 KM/H
MINIMUM CENTRAL PRESSURE...1006 MB...29.71 INCHES
 
 
WATCHES AND WARNINGS
--------------------
There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect.
 
Interests in the Hawaiian Islands should closely monitor the
progress of this system. Watches may be required for a portion of
the Hawaiian Islands tonight or Friday.
 
 
DISCUSSION AND OUTLOOK
----------------------
At 500 PM HST (0300 UTC), the center of Tropical Depression Two-C 
was located near latitude 12.9 North, longitude 145.0 West. The 
depression is moving toward the west-northwest near 14 mph (22 
km/h), and this general motion is expected to persist during the 
next few days. A gradual turn to the west is forecast thereafter, 
with the center of the system passing south of the Big Island of 
Hawaii this weekend, then the smaller main Hawaiian Islands early 
next week.
 
Maximum sustained winds are near 35 mph (55 km/h) with higher gusts.
Gradual strengthening is forecast over the couple of days, and the 
depression is expected become a tropical storm by tonight.
 
The estimated minimum central pressure is 1006 mb (29.71 inches).
 
 
HAZARDS AFFECTING LAND
----------------------
Key messages for Tropical Depression Two-C can be found in
the Tropical Cyclone Discussion under AWIPS header HFOTCDCP3 and
WMO header WTPA43 PHFO.
 
RAINFALL: The Tropical Depression is expected to produce rainfall 
totals of 5 to 10 inches with maximum amounts of 15 inches across 
the Big Island.  Rainfall totals of 1 to 2 inches with maximum 
amounts of 3 inches are expected on eastern Maui. For the remainder 
of the islands, 1 to 2 inches of rain are possible. This rainfall 
may produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in 
steep terrain and over areas that were affected recently by Lala.

For a complete depiction of forecast rainfall associated with 
Tropical Depression Two-C, please see the National Weather Service 
Storm Total Rainfall Graphic available at 
hurricanes.gov/graphics_cp3.shtml?rainqpf. 
 
SURF: Swells generated by the depression are expected to affect
portions of the Hawaiian Islands ths weekend, and could cause
life-threatening surf and rip current conditions. Please consult
products from your local weather office.
 
 
NEXT ADVISORY
-------------
Next complete advisory at 1100 PM HST.
 
$$
Forecaster Gibbs/Evans
item.author: nhcwebmaster@noaa.gov (NHC Webmaster)

item.title: Tropical Depression Two-C Forecast Discussion Number 3
item.description:
Issued at 500 PM HST Thu Aug 20 2026 
837 
WTPA43 PHFO 210236
TCDCP3
 
Tropical Depression Two-C Discussion Number   3
NWS Central Pacific Hurricane Center Honolulu HI   CP022026
Issued by NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL
500 PM HST Thu Aug 20 2026
  
Satellite imagery indicates that the convection associated with 
Tropical Depression Two-C has weakened slightly during the past 
several hours, with most of the deep convection positioned over the 
western semicircle. The latest subjective Dvorak intensity estimates 
from JTWC and HFO remain T2.0/30 kt and are generally consistent 
with the objective intensity estimates. Therefore, the initial 
intensity is held at 30 kt. Both NOAA and Air Force reconnaissance 
aircraft are scheduled to investigate the cyclone on Friday. 

The initial motion is estimated to be 290/12 kt, and this general 
motion is expected to persist into the weekend while the cyclone 
remains on the southern side of the subtropical ridge. A gradual 
turn toward the west is forecast later in the weekend as the ridge 
builds to the north of the system. Track guidance remains in 
generally good agreement, although some cross-track spread persists 
as the cyclone approaches and passes south of the Hawaiian Islands 
this weekend and into early next week. The updated NHC forecast 
reflects a blend of the previous forecast, ECMWF, and the GFS 
solutions, and generally lies near the northern side of the 
guidance envelope. 

Environmental conditions appear favorable for gradual strengthening 
during the next few days. The cyclone is forecast to remain over 
warm waters and within an adequately moist environment while 
vertical wind shear remains relatively weak. These conditions should 
support steady intensification as the system approaches the vicinity 
of the Hawaiian Islands. Beyond about 72 h, increasing shear and a 
progressively drier surrounding environment should induce a 
weakening trend by early next week as it passes south of the 
Hawaiian Islands. The NHC intensity forecast shows the system 
becoming a strong tropical storm this weekend, followed by gradual 
weakening, and remains near the upper end of the intensity guidance.
 
 
Key Messages:
 
1. The tropical depression is expected to strengthen while it moves 
west-northwestward toward the vicinity of the Hawaiian Islands over 
the next couple of days.
 
2. Heavy rainfall associated with Tropical Depression Two will begin 
to impact the Big Island of Hawaii late Saturday night, spreading 
westward across the remainder of the Hawaiian Islands Sunday into 
Monday. This rainfall may produce life-threatening flooding and 
mudslides, especially in steep terrain and over areas that were 
affected recently by Lala.
 
3. There is a risk of wind and wave impacts in the Hawaiian Islands 
regardless of the exact track and intensity of the system. Watches 
may be required for portions of the Hawaiian Islands by Friday and 
residents should closely monitor the latest forecast updates and 
ensure that they have their preparedness plan in place.
